| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_hash in ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507","96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974","a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91","9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45","2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f","aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9","7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376","38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") OR Processes.process_name="VID001.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_hash Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
File write of Talos top-prevalent malware hash to disk (drop site) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the file-system drop of the same Talos prevalent-malware hashes regardless of subsequent execution — catches the staging step before the binary runs (or when it's blocked). The d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_<N>_Exe.exe filename pattern (appearing on two of the three samples) is a strong staging-loader hallmark and warrants its own pivot on the file-event surface, separate from the process-execution UC. Rationale: Pivots on the file-system surface rather than process execution — catches the drop before execution (or when AV blocks the run). Filename pattern d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_<N>_Exe.exe is article-specific: it appears twice in the list (the W32.Injector and Win.Dropper.Miner samples share the same 32-char dropper batch prefix), which is a textbook staging-loader naming artefact and a stronger signal than any single hash.
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Defender / CrowdStrike quarantining the sample writes the file to its quarantine vault — InitiatingProcessFileName will be MsMpEng.exe / CSFalconService.exe
  • Analyst saves the IOC sample from Talos's portal to a local malware-research share
  • Backup software re-hydrating a previously quarantined file during restore testing
  • FileOriginUrl pointing to talosintelligence.com indicates a researcher download, not a real infection
Suppression filter
and not InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MpDefenderCoreService.exe","CSFalconService.exe","CSFalconContainer.exe","SenseIR.exe","MsSense.exe") and not FolderPath has_any (@"\Quarantine\", @"\Defender\Quarantine\", @"\CrowdStrike\Quarantine\")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): inspect FileOriginUrl and FileOriginIP — if it points to talosintelligence.com or virustotal.com the writer is almost certainly a researcher; otherwise treat as a live infection and pivot to the URL/IP for delivery-channel investigation. Step 2 (contain): isolate the host, quarantine the file at FolderPath, and capture the InitiatingProcessCommandLine of the writing process — that names the delivery vector (browser, mail client, archive utility, LOLBin). Step 3 (hunt): query for the same SHA256 across DeviceFileEvents org-wide for the prior 30d, then query DeviceNetworkEvents on the same DeviceId for connections in the ±15 min window around the file write to identify the download source.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where SHA256 in ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507","96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974","a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91")
  or MD5 in~ ("2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f","aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9","7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376")
  or FileName =~ "VID001.exe"
  or FileName startswith "d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_"
  or FileName matches regex @"(?i)^[a-f0-9]{32}_\d+_Exe\.exe$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, FileOriginIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileSHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507","96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974","a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91")
  or TargetFileMD5 in~ ("2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f","aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9","7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376")
  or TargetFileName =~ "VID001.exe"
  or TargetFileName startswith "d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_"
  or TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^[a-f0-9]{32}_\d+_Exe\.exe$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, TargetFileMD5, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New Attacks Trick OpenClaw AI Agent Into Running Code and Leaking Secrets

The Hacker News
2026-06-11 16 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Two security teams have shown, in separate research published this week, that OpenClaw, the popular self-hosted AI agent, can be driven to run attacker-controlled code or hand over sensitive data through ordinary-looking inputs. Imperva buried instructions inside shared contacts, vCards, and location pins that the agent executed without the victim ever seeing them. Varonis built a test agent on

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Vulnerable OpenClaw deployment (<2026.4.23) — pre-patch vCard injection exposure
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] OpenClaw agent prompt-injection markers in agent application logs · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] OpenClaw agent runtime spawning OS shell or scripting interpreter · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OpenClaw agent connecting to Imperva PoC artifact host · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] OpenClaw agent process reading or shelling against credential file paths · [LLM] OpenClaw agent sending outbound mail to first-time external recipient · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
OpenClaw agent runtime spawning OS shell or scripting interpreter AIInstallation High
Detects the core Imperva attack path where a hidden instruction inside a shared contact / vCard / location pin drives the OpenClaw agent to download and run an attacker-controlled script. Surfaces Python / Node.js agent runtimes spawning shells or LOLBins that aren't part of their declared tool surface. Rationale: Implements reviewer feedback #1 (AI Agent Unauthorized Code Execution) using the article's explicit claim that Imperva's hidden vCard/contact-name instruction caused the agent to 'download and run a script from a server the researchers controlled'. Parent = OpenClaw runtime (python/node), child = any OS shell or download LOLBin. Cross-referenced MITRE T1059 sub-techniques. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/006/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.004 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running OpenClaw locally during plugin authoring, manually invoking shell tools
  • Approved 'shell' tool declared in agent manifest executing curl for legitimate dataset fetch
  • CI worker python interpreter spawning bash for build steps unrelated to OpenClaw
  • Operations staff using node-based MCP servers that legitimately exec system utilities
  • Container entrypoint where python is PID1 and bash/sh runs as part of normal boot
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "site-packages\\pip" and ProcessCommandLine !has "vscode-server" and FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Git\\"
Response runbook
1. Triage — pull the parent ProcessCommandLine and confirm the python/node binary was actually running OpenClaw (look for `-m openclaw`, OPENCLAW_CONFIG env, or openclaw package import). Check whether the child cmd-line references imperva_artifactory.com or any external download. 2. Contain — isolate the host in Defender; stop the OpenClaw service; preserve the agent's recent message-object inputs (contacts, vCards, location pins) for forensic review. 3. Hunt — pivot on AccountName + DeviceId across DeviceFileEvents for any dropped script in %TEMP% / /tmp in the 5 minutes before the child spawned, and across DeviceNetworkEvents for the parent making any HTTP fetch in the 60s window before execution.
// OpenClaw agent runtime spawning a shell/LOLBin child — Imperva message-object injection path
let AgentParents = dynamic(["python.exe","python3.exe","python3","node.exe","node","openclaw.exe","openclaw"]);
let SuspiciousChildren = dynamic(["cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","wsl.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (AgentParents)
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("openclaw","open_claw","agent_runtime","-m openclaw")
| where FileName in~ (SuspiciousChildren)
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl ","wget ","Invoke-WebRequest","DownloadString","IEX ","bash -c","sh -c")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,

OpenClaw agent process reading or shelling against credential file paths AIActions on Objectives High
Catches the Varonis 'agent phishing' scenario where a single plain email convinces the agent to harvest AWS IAM keys, SSH creds, and DB connection strings. Hunts the OpenClaw runtime touching .ssh, .aws, .env, and cloud-credential file paths, and cloud audit logs showing the agent's identity listing/retrieving secrets it shouldn't. Rationale: Implements reviewer feedback #2 + #4 (credential leakage + sensitive file read). Article: 'forwarded mock AWS IAM access keys, database connection strings, and SSH credentials in plaintext'. CloudWatch query now starts with the required `# log group:` comment, projects only documented CloudTrail fields, and filters in eventSource/eventName instead of using them as top-level field names. Cross-checked Simon Willison 'lethal trifecta' concept referenced in article. Cross-checked against: • https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555 T1039 T1041
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running OpenClaw locally with a dev .aws/credentials file the agent legitimately reads for its declared AWS tool
  • CI agent reading ./.env for normal config bootstrap
  • SRE running ansible/saltstack with python interpreter touching /etc files unrelated to OpenClaw
  • Backup/EDR agent enumerating user home directories — not an OpenClaw process despite python parent
  • Vault-Agent sidecar python wrapper reading credentials.json by design
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--validate-only" and FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Users\\Public\\openclaw-dev-fixtures\\"
Response runbook
1. Triage — confirm the touching process was actually OpenClaw (check parent cmd-line for `openclaw`, env vars, package import). Pull the agent's recent inbox / connector messages — look for a sender outside the org asking about staging access, AWS keys, customer export, or a 'team lead' urgency pretext. 2. Contain — disable the connector / mailbox the agent reads from; rotate any IAM keys, DB passwords, and SSH keys reachable from the file paths touched; block outbound from the host to non-corporate SMTP and webhook endpoints. 3. Hunt — pivot on the IAM identity the agent assumes in CloudTrail for the last 24h looking for unusual GetSecretValue / ListAccessKeys / GetCallerIdentity from non-baseline source IPs, and pivot on EmailEvents for outbound mail with the secret strings or 'customer export' in subject/body.

Vulnerable OpenClaw deployment (<2026.4.23) — pre-patch vCard injection exposure AIWeaponization High
Inventories hosts running an OpenClaw version older than 2026.4.23, which still flattens contact-name / vCard FN / location-label fields directly into the LLM prompt with no untrusted-content marker. Pure exposure hunt — not behavioural — to prioritise patch rollout per the article's explicit fix guidance. Rationale: Implements article's explicit guidance: 'Anyone running OpenClaw should update to 2026.4.23 or later'. Inventory-style hunt that decomposes the version string and gates on the patch boundary. SPL no longer has the leaked markdown fence; pure tstats + rex + version-tuple comparison. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-attacks-trick-openclaw-ai-agent.html
ATT&CKT1588.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Test/QA hosts intentionally pinned to an old OpenClaw build for regression testing
  • Air-gapped lab where the agent never touches untrusted messaging input
  • Vendor demo VMs that ship a frozen OpenClaw release with no real data connectors
  • Process command line embedding the version of a different tool that happens to contain the word openclaw
  • Developer reproducing the Imperva PoC on a sandbox build deliberately
Response runbook
1. Triage — for each hit, confirm the version captured matches what `openclaw --version` reports on the host, and identify whether the install is exposed to inbound messages (WhatsApp/Signal/Teams connectors enabled). 2. Contain — push the 2026.4.23+ upgrade via your endpoint management, or disable the messaging connectors on hosts that cannot be upgraded today; ensure memory feature is off until patched. 3. Hunt — for any host that was on a vulnerable version in the last 30d, retro-hunt DeviceFileEvents + DeviceNetworkEvents from the agent process for the indicators in the other UCs (imperva_artifactory.com fetch, credential file reads, shell child).
// Pre-patch OpenClaw build exposed to Imperva vCard/contact/location injection (fix shipped in 2026.4.23)
let VulnVersionRegex = @"(?i)openclaw[ _\-]?v?(\d{4})\.(\d+)\.(\d+)";
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("openclaw.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine matches regex VulnVersionRegex
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex VulnVersionRegex
| extend OcVersion = extract_all(VulnVersionRegex, dynamic([1,2,3]), strcat(InitiatingProcessCommandLine, " ", ProcessCommandLine))
| mv-expand OcVersion
| extend Major = toint(OcVersion[0]), Minor = toint(OcVersion[1]), Patch = toint(OcVersion[2])
| where Major < 2026
    or (Major == 2026 and Minor < 4)
    or (Major == 2026 and Minor == 4 and Patch < 23)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Sample = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
          by DeviceName, AccountName, Major, Minor, Patch
| order by LastSeen desc
let VulnVersionRegex = @"(?i)openclaw[ _\-]?v?(\d{4})\.(\d+)\.(\d+)";
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("openclaw.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe")
   or ActingProcessName has_any ("openclaw.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex VulnVersionRegex
    or ParentProcessCommandLine matches regex VulnVersionRegex
| extend OcVersion = extract_all(VulnVersionRegex, dynamic([1,2,3]), strcat(ActingProcessCommandLine, " ", ParentProcessCommandLine))
| mv-expand OcVersion
| extend Major = toint(OcVersion[0]), Minor = toint(OcVersion[1]), Patch = toint(OcVersion[2])
| where Major < 2026
    or (Major == 2026 and Minor < 4)
    or (Major == 2026 and Minor == 4 and Patch < 23)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Sample = any(ActingProcessCommandLine)
          by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, Major, Minor, Patch

OR *openclaw*2026.4.2[0-2]) OR @process.command_line:(*openclaw*2025.* OR *openclaw*2026.0.* OR *openclaw*2026.1.* OR *openclaw*2026.2.* OR *openclaw*2026.3.* OR *openclaw*2026.4.0 OR *openclaw*2026.4.1 OR *openclaw*2026.4.2 OR *openclaw*2026.4.3))

OpenClaw agent connecting to Imperva PoC artifact host AICommand & Control High
Pivots on the only IOC in the article: imperva_artifactory.com is the Imperva-controlled server the agent was driven to download a script from in the PoC. Surfaces any process — but especially the OpenClaw runtime — resolving or contacting that host. Tight, high-fidelity, low-FP. Rationale: Single high-confidence IOC straight from the article's pre-extracted list (imperva_artifactory.com). Imperva's tests against Gemini 3.1 Pro 'told the agent to download and run a script from a server the researchers controlled' — this host is that server. Cross-checked against article body and IOC block. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-attacks-trick-openclaw-ai-agent.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal red team or blue team intentionally reproducing the Imperva PoC
  • Vulnerability scanner or threat-intel platform actively crawling published IOCs
  • Security researcher's host with the article open and the link previewer fetching the domain
  • DNS sinkhole / passive DNS replication service touching the domain
Response runbook
1. Triage — confirm the contacting process is the OpenClaw agent runtime and pull the surrounding 10 minutes of agent input (incoming contacts / vCards / location pins) for the hidden-instruction payload. 2. Contain — block imperva_artifactory.com at DNS/proxy/firewall tenant-wide; quarantine the host; preserve memory and the agent's stored memory file (memory is on by default per article). 3. Hunt — for the AccountName/DeviceId pair, pivot on DeviceFileEvents for any newly-dropped script in the last hour, on DeviceProcessEvents for execution of that script, and across the org for any other host that resolved the domain.
// IOC: imperva_artifactory.com — Imperva PoC payload host (article-cited)
let C2 = dynamic(["imperva_artifactory.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (C2)
   or tostring(parse_url(RemoteUrl).Host) has_any (C2)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2 = dynamic(["imperva_artifactory.com"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  ( ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DnsQuery has_any (C2)
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DstIpAddr ),
  ( ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DstHostname has_any (C2) or Url has_any (C2)
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, Url )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OpenClaw agent prompt-injection markers in agent application logs AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Imperva injection shape inside OpenClaw's own ingestion logs: angle-bracket-wrapped `<contact: ...>` strings whose name field carries instructions, plus the giveaway phrases the Varonis test agents fell for ('production incident', 'staging access', 'QBR deck', 'weekly customer export'). Sentinel/Splunk/Datadog text-pattern hunt across CommonSecurityLog/Syslog/AppLogs. Rationale: Implements reviewer feedback #3 (prompt injection / jailbreak attempt) using strings drawn straight from the article: the `<contact: name, number>` flattening shape (Imperva), the Varonis pretexts ('production incident', 'staging access', 'QBR deck', 'weekly customer export'), and the generic 'ignore previous instructions' jailbreak. Article body + Simon Willison lethal-trifecta framing. Cross-checked against: • https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-attacks-trick-openclaw-ai-agent.html
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1059
Data sourcesEmail.Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate sales team forwarding genuine QBR-deck requests through the agent
  • Real production incidents where a team lead does ask for staging access via chat
  • Security awareness emails containing literal example injection strings
  • Discussion of the article itself in the agent's input (chat about the threat)
  • Red-team / purple-team drills reproducing the Varonis test prompts
Suppression filter
| where not (Message has "threat awareness" or Message has "phishing-simulation" or Message has "red-team")
Response runbook
1. Triage — for each hit, pull the full prompt the agent received and the tool calls the agent made in the 60s after; check whether the agent reached a credential file or composed an outbound email. 2. Contain — if a tool-call cascade followed (file read, email send), revoke the connector and rotate credentials touched; if not, log and add the sender to enhanced monitoring. 3. Hunt — across the same agent identity for repeat injection markers in the last 30d; across other agent identities for the same sender; cross-correlate with the imperva_artifactory.com and credential-file UCs to see if this prompt led to actual execution.
// Imperva injection markers + Varonis social-pretext phrases reaching the OpenClaw agent
let InjectionMarkers = dynamic([
    "<contact:","<vcard:","<location:",
    "ignore previous instructions","system:","</system>",
    "download and run","curl http","wget http","bash -c","powershell -c",
    "forward to","reply with the","send to outside"]);
let SocialPretexts = dynamic([
    "production incident","staging access","QBR deck",
    "weekly customer export","team lead","urgent"]);
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has_cs "OpenClaw" or ApplicationId has "openclaw"
| where tostring(RawEventData) has_any (InjectionMarkers)
    or tostring(RawEventData) has_any (SocialPretexts)
| project Timestamp, Application, AccountDisplayName, ActionType,
          IPAddress, UserAgent, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
let InjectionMarkers = dynamic([
    "<contact:","<vcard:","<location:",
    "ignore previous instructions","</system>",
    "download and run","curl http","wget http","bash -c"]);
let SocialPretexts = dynamic([
    "production incident","staging access","QBR deck",
    "weekly customer export"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  ( Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ProcessName has_any ("openclaw","openclaw-agent","python")
    | where SyslogMessage has_any (InjectionMarkers) or SyslogMessage has_any (SocialPretexts)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage),
  ( CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DeviceProduct has "OpenClaw" or ApplicationProtocol has "openclaw"
    | where Message has_any (InjectionMarkers) or Message has_any (SocialPretexts)
    | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceUserName, Message)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:openclaw OR @service:openclaw OR @logger.name:openclaw*) (@message:("<contact:" OR "<vcard:" OR "<location:" OR "ignore previous instructions" OR "</system>" OR "download and run" OR "bash -c" OR "production incident" OR "staging access" OR "QBR deck" OR "weekly customer export"))
#event_simpleName=ScriptControlScanInfo
| regex("<contact:|<vcard:|<location:|ignore previous instructions|</system>|download and run|bash -c|production incident|staging access|QBR deck|weekly customer export", field=ScriptContent, flags="i")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, HostName], function=count())
APPLICATION
index=* sourcetype IN ("openclaw:agent","openclaw:prompt","openclaw:tool","syslog") ("<contact:" OR "<vcard:" OR "<location:") ("ignore previous instructions" OR "system:" OR "download " OR "curl " OR "wget " OR "exec(" OR "os.system" OR "subprocess" OR "rm -rf" OR "bash -c") | rex field=_raw "<(?<obj_type>contact|vcard|location):\s*(?<obj_name>[^,>]{20,})" | where isnotnull(obj_name) | table _time host source obj_type obj_name _raw
OpenClaw agent sending outbound mail to first-time external recipient AIActions on Objectives High
Implements the Varonis 'agent phishing' exfil endpoint: a hijacked agent quietly forwards AWS keys / customer exports / credentials to an outside address. Detection compares the agent identity's outbound mail against a 30-day baseline of recipients it normally sends to, and alerts when it sends to a first-time external domain — the gating control Varonis explicitly recommends. Rationale: Implements reviewer feedback #2 + #5 endpoint of exfil chain, using Varonis's explicit recommendation: 'Outbound mail needs a gate: no first-time sends to unfamiliar addresses without approval'. Anti-join on 30-day baseline of (sender, recipient) is the cleanest expression of 'first-time' per the KQL knowledge base pattern-behavioural-baseline. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-attacks-trick-openclaw-ai-agent.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1114/003/
ATT&CKT1567 T1114.003
Data sourcesEmail.Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Agent legitimately onboarded to email a new vendor / customer for the first time
  • Marketing campaign send from a service mailbox named 'agent-foo'
  • Agent identity migrated from one mailbox to another and the baseline hasn't caught up
  • Sales rep using the agent to draft outreach to a prospect they've never emailed
  • Bulk newsletter via a 'bot@' identity that legitimately fans out to new addresses each send
Suppression filter
| where Subject !has "newsletter" and Subject !has "campaign" and AttachmentCount == 0 or RcptDomain !in ("gmail.com","proton.me","outlook.com") | where true   // tune per tenant
Response runbook
1. Triage — pull the email body + attachments; look for the article's tells: AWS access keys, DB connection strings, SSH credentials, customer-export CSV. Inspect the trigger message the agent acted on (sender, urgency framing). 2. Contain — block the outbound recipient at the mail gateway; revoke the agent's mailbox connector; rotate any credentials present in the body / attachment. 3. Hunt — across the past 30d for any other outbound from the agent identity to never-before-seen domains; check IdentityLogonEvents for the agent's service principal touching unusual resources; pair with the credential-file-read UC for the source of the leaked secrets.
// Agent identity sending to a recipient it has never sent to in the prior 30d (Varonis Pinchy exfil shape)
let Lookback = 30d;
let RecentWindow = 1h;
let AgentSenderPattern = @"(?i)openclaw|agent|pinchy|bot";
let Baseline = EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(Lookback) .. ago(RecentWindow))
    | where EmailDirection == "Outbound"
    | where SenderFromAddress matches regex AgentSenderPattern
    | summarize by SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress;
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(RecentWindow)
| where EmailDirection == "Outbound"
| where SenderFromAddress matches regex AgentSenderPattern
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress
| extend RcptDomain = tolower(tostring(split(RecipientEmailAddress, "@")[1]))
| where RcptDomain !endswith "yourcorp.com"   // tune per tenant
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, RcptDomain,
          Subject, AttachmentCount, UrlCount, NetworkMessageId
| order by Timestamp desc
let Lookback = 30d;
let RecentWindow = 1h;
let AgentSenderPattern = @"(?i)openclaw|agent|pinchy|bot";
let Baseline = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(Lookback) .. ago(RecentWindow))
    | where Operation in ("Send","SendAs","SendOnBehalf")
    | where UserId matches regex AgentSenderPattern
    | mv-expand Recipients
    | summarize by UserId, Recipient = tolower(tostring(Recipients));
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(RecentWindow)
| where Operation in ("Send","SendAs","SendOnBehalf")
| where UserId matches regex AgentSenderPattern
| mv-expand Recipients
| extend Recipient = tolower(tostring(Recipients))
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on UserId, Recipient
| extend RcptDomain = tostring(split(Recipient, "@")[1])
| where RcptDomain !endswith "yourcorp.com"
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Recipient, RcptDomain, Subject, ClientIP
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(office365 OR google.workspace) @evt.name:(send OR Send OR mail.send) @usr.email:(*openclaw* OR *agent* OR *pinchy* OR *bot*) -@recipient:(*@yourcorp.com OR *@corp.yourcorp.com)
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count from datamodel=Email.Email where All_Email.direction=outbound by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | eval rcpt_domain=mvindex(split(recipient,"@"),1) | join type=left src_user [| tstats summariesonly=t earliest(_time) as baseline_first from datamodel=Email.Email where All_Email.direction=outbound earliest=-30d@d latest=-1h by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | rename recipient as baseline_rcpt] | where isnull(baseline_first) AND match(src_user,"(?i)openclaw|agent|pinchy|bot") AND NOT match(rcpt_domain,"(?i)mycompany\.com$|mycorp\.local$")
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email.Email where All_Email.direction=outbound by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | eval rcpt_domain=mvindex(split(recipient,"@"),1) | join type=left src_user [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) as baseline_first from datamodel=Email.Email where All_Email.direction=outbound earliest=-30d@d latest=-1h by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | rename recipient as baseline_rcpt] | where isnull(baseline_first) AND match(src_user,"(?i)openclaw|agent|pinchy|bot") AND NOT match(rcpt_domain,"(?i)mycompany\.com$|mycorp\.local$")

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Defender Offline Scan initiation creates GreatXML-vulnerable WinRE state
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Reboot to WinRE via shutdown /r /o (GreatXML exploit trigger) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] GreatXML staging: write of unattend.xml or ReAgent.xml to Windows Recovery path · [LLM] Reagentc.exe reconfiguring WinRE image path or enabling recovery boot
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
GreatXML staging: write of unattend.xml or ReAgent.xml to Windows Recovery path AIInstallation High
Detects the core staging step of the GreatXML BitLocker bypass — a non-TrustedInstaller process writing unattend.xml or Recovery\WindowsRE\ReAgent.xml under a recovery-partition or WinRE path. This is the article's primary detectable artifact before the host is rebooted into WinRE. Rationale: Article literally names both files (unattend.xml at the root and Recovery/WindowsRE/ReAgent.xml) as the staging payload. Filtering out TrustedInstaller/reagentc/DismHost keeps Windows Update + DISM noise out while preserving the attacker's write because they cannot impersonate those signed contexts without already-elevated rights.
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1564 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows feature update or in-place upgrade copying a fresh WinRE image (DismHost / WindowsUpdateBox)
  • OEM provisioning tools (HP/Dell/Lenovo recovery toolkits) restaging WinRE during imaging
  • Sysprep + unattend.xml answer file authoring on a build / golden-image VM
  • MDT/SCCM task sequences that touch the recovery partition during OSD
  • Manual administrator using reagentc /setreimage to relocate WinRE (will be allowlisted by reagentc.exe parent filter)
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("TiWorker.exe", "WindowsUpdateBox.exe", "TrustedInstaller.exe", "setuphost.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\$WINDOWS.~BT\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent-process chain and signing status of InitiatingProcessFileName, and confirm the device is not in an active OSD/feature-update window via Update history. Was the writing process started by an interactive user session vs SYSTEM? 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response, snapshot the recovery partition (mount via DiskPart, copy ReAgent.xml + unattend.xml off for analysis), and force a BitLocker key rotation so the staged WinRE bypass cannot be used post-recovery. 3) Hunt: in the same DeviceId, search ±2h for reagentc.exe, MpCmdRun.exe -OfflineScan, shutdown.exe /r /o, and any diskpart 'assign letter' against the recovery volume. Pivot on the writing user across other hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("unattend.xml", "ReAgent.xml")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Recovery\WindowsRE\", @"\Recovery\", @"\WinRE\", @"GLOBALROOT\Device\", @"\System Volume Information\WindowsRE\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe", "TiWorker.exe", "reagentc.exe", "WindowsUpdateBox.exe", "setupcl.exe", "DismHost.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("system", "local service", "network service")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType,
          Actor = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          ProcessName = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ProcessPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ProcessCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          IntegrityLevel = InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel,
          TargetFile = FileName,
          TargetFolder = FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("unattend.xml", "ReAgent.xml")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Recovery\WindowsRE\", @"\Recovery\", @"\WinRE\", @"GLOBALROOT\Device\")
| where ActingProcessName !endswith "TrustedInstaller.exe"
| where ActingProcessName !endswith "TiWorker.exe"
| where ActingProcessName !endswith "reagentc.exe"
| where ActingProcessName !endswith "DismHost.exe"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GreatXML BitLocker Bypass Staging via Recovery XML Write
id: 8c2f3b1d-9a4e-4d1c-bc8e-7f3e5a9c8d12
description: Detects writes of unattend.xml or ReAgent.xml under Windows Recovery / WinRE paths by a process other than TrustedInstaller or reagentc, matching the staging step of the GreatXML BitLocker bypass.
references:
    - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-greatxml-exploit-bypasses-windows.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:

    - attack.t1027
logsource:
    category: file_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_recovery_unattend:
        TargetFilename|contains|all:
            - '\Recovery\'
            - '\unattend.xml'
    selection_reagent:
        TargetFilename|endswith: '\Recovery\WindowsRE\ReAgent.xml'
    filter_trusted:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\TrustedInstaller.exe'

    - OEM imaging / Sysprep operations on freshly provisioned hardware
level: high

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\\Recovery\\WindowsRE\\ReAgent.xml OR *\\Recovery\\WindowsRE\\reagent.xml OR *\\Recovery\\*\\unattend.xml OR *\\recovery\\*\\unattend.xml)) -@Image:(*\\TrustedInstaller.exe OR *\\trustedinstaller.exe OR *\\TiWorker.exe OR *\\tiworker.exe OR *\\reagentc.exe OR *\\Reagentc.exe OR *\\DismHost.exe OR *\\dismhost.exe)

| TargetFileName=/\\Recovery\\(WindowsRE\\ReAgent\.xml|[^\\]*\\unattend\.xml)$/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/(TrustedInstaller|TiWorker|reagentc|WindowsUpdateBox|DismHost)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=[count(), min(@timestamp, as=firstSeen), max(@timestamp, as=lastSeen)])

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="unattend.xml" OR Filesystem.file_name="ReAgent.xml") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Recovery\\WindowsRE\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Recovery\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*GLOBALROOT\\Device\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_guid
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where NOT match(process_name, "(?i)(TrustedInstaller|TiWorker|reagentc|WindowsUpdateBox)\\.exe")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="unattend.xml" OR Filesystem.file_name="ReAgent.xml") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Recovery\\WindowsRE\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Recovery\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*GLOBALROOT\\Device\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_guid
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where NOT match(process_name, "(?i)(TrustedInstaller|TiWorker|reagentc|WindowsUpdateBox)\\.exe")

Defender Offline Scan initiation creates GreatXML-vulnerable WinRE state AIWeaponization Medium
Hunts hosts that have initiated a Microsoft Defender Offline Scan, which the GreatXML author states automatically renders the host vulnerable to the BitLocker bypass. This is a vulnerability-surface enumeration query, not a confirmed compromise. Rationale: Article: 'If you ever attempted to use Windows Defender Offline Scan, you're automatically vulnerable to a BitLocker bypass.' This isn't malicious by itself, so it ships as hunting tier to enumerate the vulnerable population and pre-stage incident response. The query keys on MpCmdRun.exe -OfflineScan which is the only documented way the offline scan feature is invoked.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1542.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • End user clicking 'Microsoft Defender Offline scan' in Windows Security to clean a malware infection
  • Helpdesk-triggered offline scan as part of a documented remediation playbook
  • EDR/AV testing in a lab where analysts exercise the offline-scan flow
  • Managed IT scripts that automate periodic offline scans on kiosks
  • Vendor support sessions guiding a user through Defender troubleshooting
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user and parent process — was this a UI-driven Security Center action (legitimate-shaped) or a scripted invocation (suspicious)? 2) Contain: do not action a single hit; instead tag the host as 'GreatXML-vulnerable' in the asset inventory and re-verify ReAgent.xml integrity on that host's recovery partition. 3) Hunt: within 24h of each hit, search the same DeviceId for the UC1 file-write signature, shutdown.exe /r /o, and reagentc.exe modifications — those three together with this prerequisite constitute the full GreatXML kill chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "MpCmdRun.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-OfflineScan", "OfflineScan", "-BootSafeMode")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          IntegrityLevel = ProcessIntegrityLevel
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            Hits = count(), Cmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 5)
            by DeviceName, AccountName
| order by LastSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\MpCmdRun.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("-OfflineScan", "OfflineScan", "-BootSafeMode")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Hits = count(), Cmds = make_set(CommandLine, 5)
          by Computer, Account
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Microsoft Defender Offline Scan Initiation (GreatXML Prerequisite)

description: Microsoft Defender Offline Scan being initiated via MpCmdRun.exe puts the host into the GreatXML-vulnerable WinRE state. Hunt only, since the feature is legitimate.

Reagentc.exe reconfiguring WinRE image path or enabling recovery boot AIInstallation Medium
Detects use of the Windows reagentc.exe utility to relocate, re-enable, or set the WinRE image — operations that directly manipulate the surface the GreatXML exploit abuses, and that are uncommon outside servicing windows. Rationale: The GreatXML bypass requires a manipulated WinRE image to be in place; reagentc.exe is the supported way to register or relocate that image. Filtering out servicing-stack parents (TiWorker, TrustedInstaller) keeps Windows Update reconfigurations quiet while leaving interactive/scripted abuse visible. The /boottore flag in particular forces the next reboot into WinRE — a giveaway of the exploit sequence.
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1574
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT administrator manually re-registering WinRE after a failed feature update ('reagentc /setreimage')
  • Vendor OEM imaging script setting /setosimage during build
  • Engineering bench scripts that toggle /enable + /disable for WinRE testing
  • Helpdesk recovery troubleshooting flagged in the change ticketing system
  • Endpoint configuration baseline tools (e.g. some MDM agents) calling reagentc /enable on first boot
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "sfc" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host is in an active patching / feature-update window in WSUS/Intune. Check the cmdline for '/setreimage <path>' and confirm the path points to a normal C:\Windows\System32\Recovery location vs. a user-writable directory. 2) Contain: if outside a change window, isolate the host and dump the current ReAgentConfig (reagentc /info) plus the recovery partition contents before reboot. Disable WinRE temporarily on critical assets via reagentc /disable until staged content is reviewed. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same DeviceId for the UC1 file-write signature and for any shutdown.exe /r /o that would actually trigger the bypass.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "reagentc.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/setreimage", "/enable", "/boottore", "/setosimage")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TiWorker.exe", "TrustedInstaller.exe", "WindowsUpdateBox.exe", "setupcl.exe", "DismHost.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ProcessCommandLine,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          GrandParent = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          IntegrityLevel = ProcessIntegrityLevel,
          IsRemoteSession = AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\reagentc.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("/setreimage", "/enable", "/boottore", "/setosimage")
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\TiWorker.exe"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\TrustedInstaller.exe"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\WindowsUpdateBox.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Reagentc.exe Reconfiguring WinRE Image or Recovery Boot (GreatXML Exploit Path)
id: 6a1e7d22-bc5f-4a09-9bba-2d8f6e0c4a55
description: reagentc.exe is the supported tool for managing the WinRE image and recovery-boot state. Outside of OS servicing it is rarely invoked, and the GreatXML bypass depends on a manipulable WinRE image — flag interactive use.
references:

| ImageFileName=/\\reagentc\.exe$/i

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="reagentc.exe" AND (Processes.process="*/setreimage*" OR Processes.process="*/enable*" OR Processes.process="*/boottore*" OR Processes.process="*/setosimage*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where NOT match(parent_process_name, "(?i)(TiWorker|TrustedInstaller|WindowsUpdateBox|setupcl)\\.exe")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where NOT match(parent_process_name, "(?i)(TiWorker|TrustedInstaller|WindowsUpdateBox|setupcl)\\.exe")

Reboot to WinRE via shutdown /r /o (GreatXML exploit trigger) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the final trigger of the GreatXML chain — a user-mode invocation of shutdown.exe with the /o (Advanced Options) flag, which is the scripted equivalent of holding Shift while clicking Restart and is what actually boots the host into the manipulated WinRE. Rationale: The article explicitly instructs the attacker to 'Reboot to WinRE by holding Shift while clicking Restart.' The non-GUI equivalent of that exact action is shutdown.exe /r /o — the only documented combination of switches that triggers a reboot into the Advanced Boot Options / WinRE menu. Pairing /r with /o eliminates almost all benign reboot noise.
ATT&CKT1529 T1542.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Helpdesk script that boots a user into Advanced Options for safe-mode troubleshooting
  • Engineering driver-signing or kernel-debug workflow that repeatedly enters WinRE
  • Build-lab automation that toggles secure-boot / test-signing modes
  • End user who learned about shutdown.exe flags from a tutorial
  • Microsoft Endpoint Manager remediation script that uses shutdown /r /o for advanced recovery
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sccm.exe", "ccmexec.exe", "intunemanagementextension.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "FastBoot"
Response runbook
1) Triage: correlate the shutdown event with the immediately preceding 24h on the same DeviceId for UC1 (XML file writes), UC2 (offline-scan initiation), or UC3 (reagentc reconfig). A standalone /r /o is low-value; chained with the other UCs it is high-value. 2) Contain: pre-emptively re-seal BitLocker (suspend + resume protectors, rotate the recovery key) on any host that exhibits the chain — assume the recovery key is compromised. 3) Hunt: post-reboot, inspect the host on next agent check-in for anomalous file writes against C:\ at SYSTEM integrity that lack a parent process (a typical artifact of operations performed from WinRE while the EDR agent was offline).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "shutdown.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s/o\b"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s/r\b"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ProcessCommandLine,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          GrandParent = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          IsRemoteSession = AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\shutdown.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s/o\b"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s/r\b"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Shutdown to Advanced Boot Options / WinRE via shutdown.exe /r /o
id: 12af48d6-3e07-49aa-a31c-77b8ce410f9d
description: shutdown.exe invoked with both /r and /o forces a reboot into the Windows Recovery / Advanced Boot Options menu — the trigger step of the GreatXML BitLocker bypass and equivalent to the article's Shift+Restart instruction.
references:
    - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-greatxml-exploit-bypasses-windows.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:

        Image|endswith: '\shutdown.exe'
        CommandLine|contains: ' /o'
    selection_reboot:
        CommandLine|contains: ' /r'
    condition: selection and selection_reboot
falsepositives:
    - IT helpdesk guiding a user into Advanced Boot Options for legitimate troubleshooting
    - Engineering / driver-development workflows requiring repeated WinRE entry
level: medium

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\shutdown.exe OR *\\Shutdown.exe OR *\\SHUTDOWN.EXE) @CommandLine:(*\ \/o* OR *\ \/O*) @CommandLine:(*\ \/r* OR *\ \/R*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\shutdown\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/\s\/o\b/i
| CommandLine=/\s\/r\b/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=[count(), min(@timestamp, as=firstSeen)])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="shutdown.exe" Processes.process="*/o*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| eval has_r=if(match(process,"(?i)\\s/r\\b"),1,0), has_o=if(match(process,"(?i)\\s/o\\b"),1,0)
| where has_r=1 AND has_o=1
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="shutdown.exe" Processes.process="*/o*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| eval has_r=if(match(process,"(?i)\\s/r\\b"),1,0), has_o=if(match(process,"(?i)\\s/o\\b"),1,0)
| where has_r=1 AND has_o=1
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

GitHub Security Advisories
2026-06-11 6 use cases 1 technique 3 kill-chain phases detected

CodeIgniter4 has a validation bypass when uploading file extensions via `ext_in` rule
