Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.

Unauthenticated POST to meta-ads-mcp /mcp endpoint on TCP 8080 (CVE-2026-48039) AIExploitation High
Hunts for inbound HTTP POSTs to the /mcp endpoint on TCP 8080 that succeed without an Authorization header — the exact exploitation vector for CVE-2026-48039 where AuthInjectionMiddleware.dispatch() forwards unauthenticated requests to downstream MCP tool handlers. Correlates with successful 200 responses to confirm tool execution rather than rejection. Rationale: Article body explicitly names the /mcp endpoint, TCP 8080 default port, and POST verb in its PoC (docker run -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 ... POST /mcp HTTP/1.1). Combination of POST + /mcp + 8080 + 200 status + external source is the exploitation signature with near-zero benign baseline. No external sources cross-checked — advisory is the canonical source.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal monitoring/healthcheck POSTs from the same subnet (filter by src IP allow-list)
  • Authorized red-team or vulnerability scans against the MCP server
  • CI/CD integration tests hitting /mcp from a known build-runner IP
  • Authenticated MCP clients that don't strip the Authorization header but proxy strips it before logging
  • Internal misconfiguration where MCP is intentionally exposed to a trusted internal segment
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--host 127.0.0.1" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--host localhost" and RemoteIP !in (dynamic(["<known-monitoring-ip-1>","<known-scanner-ip-1>"]))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Pull the full request body and response for the matching session — confirm the JSON-RPC `tools/call` method invocation and inspect the response body for the substring `access_token=` in any `request_url` field (proof of token leakage). Identify the source IP, geo, and ASN; check threat-intel reputation. 2. Contain: Immediately block inbound 8080 from external networks at the perimeter firewall; if the meta-ads-mcp container is exposed (--host 0.0.0.0), restart with --host 127.0.0.1 binding or place behind an authenticated reverse proxy. Rotate the operator's META_ACCESS_TOKEN in Meta Business Manager and revoke any active sessions. 3. Hunt: Search outbound traffic from the host to graph.facebook.com for any URL containing `access_token=` (UC2); review Meta Ads activity log for unauthorized ad-account API calls during the exposure window; check for other exposed MCP servers in the estate via UC3.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName

Meta Graph API outbound URL leaking access_token in query string AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for outbound HTTPS to graph.facebook.com with `access_token=` exposed as a URL query parameter — the api.py:136 vulnerability where meta-ads-mcp appends the operator token directly to the URL rather than using an Authorization header. Captured when proxy TLS inspection is enabled or via host-side process command-line / script-content telemetry. Both pre-error (every Graph call) and post-error (token echoed back to attacker) cases are covered. Rationale: Article shows the exact leakage shape: `request_url`: `https://graph.facebook.com/v24.0/me/adaccounts?...&access_token=FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO_123456789`, and api.py:136 confirms the token is appended as a URL query param on every call. Detecting `graph.facebook.com` + `access_token=` in a URL is high-fidelity — Meta's documented best practice is Authorization header, so seeing the token in a URL is itself a misconfiguration signal.
ATT&CKT1041 T1552.001 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy applications still using URL-based Graph API auth (Meta deprecated this pattern but it remains in some SDKs)
  • Developer/QA boxes running ad-hoc curl tests against Graph API
  • Marketing-automation tools that have not migrated to OAuth Bearer headers
  • Logging/observability pipelines that scrub URLs but echo the original in error messages
  • Proxy logs that capture the URL before redaction policies apply
Suppression filter
| where Url !has "client_id=" and Url !has "/oauth/access_token" and ActorUsername !in (dynamic(["<dev-test-account-1>","<known-marketing-svc>"]))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Extract the full URL and the captured `token_prefix`; cross-reference against the known operator token prefix (consult the Meta Business Manager admin to confirm which prefix maps to the production META_ACCESS_TOKEN). Identify the originating host and process. 2. Contain: Rotate the affected META_ACCESS_TOKEN immediately via Meta Business Manager — long-lived tokens are valid for 60 days. Audit any client of meta-ads-mcp that may have received the token in a JSON-RPC response. 3. Hunt: Search Meta Ads API audit logs (via Graph API `/me/business_users` activity) for actions performed by this token from non-corporate IPs in the last 30 days; look for spend manipulation, new ad-account permissions, or audience exports. Pivot to UC1 to find the unauthenticated /mcp POST that triggered the leak.

meta-ads-mcp listener bound to non-loopback interface (0.0.0.0:8080) AIInstallation High
Hunts for meta-ads-mcp processes that bind the HTTP MCP listener to a non-loopback interface (--host 0.0.0.0, --host *, or any non-127.0.0.1 address on port 8080) — the deployment-level misconfiguration that exposes the CVE-2026-48039 vulnerable endpoint to the network. Loopback-only bindings are out of scope; this catches the prerequisite for remote exploitation. Rationale: Article impact section states 'an unauthenticated attacker who can reach the MCP server's HTTP port (default 8080)' — the prerequisite is non-loopback exposure. PoC shows the safe loopback binding (`-p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080`) which intentionally limits exposure; we detect the opposite. Process-command-line pattern `meta_ads_mcp` + `--host 0.0.0.0` is article-grounded and high-fidelity.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Intentional deployment behind an authenticated reverse proxy where 0.0.0.0 binding is required for the proxy to reach the container (verify the proxy enforces auth)
  • Kubernetes pods where service mesh fronts the listener (binding is 0.0.0.0 but ingress is gated)
  • Internal lab/test deployments where exposure is bounded by network segmentation
  • Developer workstations running local dev containers (--host 0.0.0.0 is common but should not be allowed in production VLANs)
  • CI integration runners spinning up the server briefly for tests
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "--reverse-proxy" and DeviceName !in (dynamic(["<dev-workstation-1>","<ci-runner-1>"]))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Confirm the bind interface and port from the process command line; check `netstat -tlnp` / `ss -tlnp` (or `Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen`) to verify 8080 is actually listening on the public interface. Identify whether the host has a public IP or is behind a NAT/proxy. 2. Contain: Restart the meta-ads-mcp service with `--host 127.0.0.1` (loopback only) and place behind an authenticated reverse proxy (nginx + bearer-token auth, Traefik with forward-auth, or similar). Block inbound 8080 at the host firewall. 3. Hunt: Pivot to UC1 to check whether any external POST has already hit /mcp during the exposure window; pivot to UC2 to check whether the operator token has been seen in outbound URLs; check the version (UC4) to confirm whether the running build is in the ≤1.0.101 vulnerable range.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("meta_ads_mcp","meta-ads-mcp")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--host 0.0.0.0","--host *","--host 0","-h 0.0.0.0","HOST=0.0.0.0")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--port 8080" and ProcessCommandLine !has "127.0.0.1" and ProcessCommandLine !has "localhost" and ProcessCommandLine !has "::1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("meta_ads_mcp","meta-ads-mcp") or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("meta_ads_mcp","meta-ads-mcp")
| extend CmdLine = coalesce(TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine)
| where CmdLine has_any ("--host 0.0.0.0","--host *","HOST=0.0.0.0","-h 0.0.0.0")
   or (CmdLine has "--port 8080" and CmdLine !has "127.0.0.1" and CmdLine !has "localhost")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, CmdLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable meta-ads-mcp version (<=1.0.108) inventory AIReconnaissance High
Identifies hosts running meta-ads-mcp in the vulnerable range (≤1.0.101 confirmed; 1.0.102–1.0.108 lack git tags and are unconfirmed-patch) via software inventory and process command-line version banners. Output feeds an asset-priority list for patching and feeds UC3 to flag the highest-risk hosts (vulnerable version + non-loopback binding). Rationale: Article explicitly states 'Affected version: ≤ 1.0.101' and 'vuln <= 1.0.108' in the package footer. Version regex `^1\.0\.([0-9]|[1-9][0-9]|10[0-8])$` matches the precise vulnerable range. Pulling from both TVM software inventory and live process command-lines gives both the dormant-install and actively-running signal — important because pip-installed packages can be present but not running.
ATT&CKT1518 T1592.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Versions 1.0.102–1.0.105 may be patched but cannot be confirmed without git tags — these will surface as potential vulnerable even if actually safe
  • Developer/CI hosts intentionally pinning an old version for regression testing
  • Vendored copies of meta-ads-mcp inside Docker base images where the image hasn't been rebuilt
  • Shadow IT installs where meta-ads-mcp was pulled into a venv outside the central inventory
  • Hosts with old `pip freeze` snapshots in inventory that no longer reflect current state
Response runbook
1. Triage: Cross-reference the output with UC3 to identify hosts that are both vulnerable AND exposed on a non-loopback interface — these are highest priority. Sort by LastSeen to find currently-running instances. 2. Contain: For exposed+vulnerable hosts, immediately apply the workaround (bind to 127.0.0.1 only, or block inbound 8080) and schedule emergency patching to ≥1.0.109 (next confirmed-fixed version per the advisory wording). 3. Hunt: For each vulnerable host, pull 90 days of UC1 (inbound /mcp POSTs) and UC2 (outbound graph.facebook.com URLs with access_token=) to establish whether exploitation has already occurred. Rotate META_ACCESS_TOKEN on any host where indicators are positive.
let VulnVersionRegex = @"^1\.0\.([0-9]|[1-9][0-9]|10[0-8])$";
let FromInventory = DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
  | where SoftwareName has_any ("meta-ads-mcp","meta_ads_mcp") or (SoftwareVendor =~ "pipeboard" and SoftwareName has "mcp")
  | where SoftwareVersion matches regex VulnVersionRegex
  | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, Source="TVM", SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion;
let FromProcess = DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("meta_ads_mcp","meta-ads-mcp")
  | extend SoftwareVersion = extract(@"meta[_-]ads[_-]mcp[^0-9]*([0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
  | where isnotempty(SoftwareVersion) and SoftwareVersion matches regex VulnVersionRegex
  | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, Source="Process", SoftwareName="meta-ads-mcp", SoftwareVersion;
union FromInventory, FromProcess
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Sources=make_set(Source), Versions=make_set(SoftwareVersion) by DeviceId, DeviceName
| order by LastSeen desc

CVE-2026-48039 PoC artifact execution (docker image meta-ads-mcp-vuln001, FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO) AIExploitation High
Detects known public-PoC artifacts for CVE-2026-48039: the `meta-ads-mcp-vuln001` Docker image referenced in the advisory PoC, the literal `FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO_123456789` placeholder token shipped in the PoC environment, and execution of `poc.py` invoking the /mcp endpoint. High-confidence signal of either red-team testing or naive attacker tooling that hasn't customised the PoC. Rationale: Article PoC section names the exact strings: docker image `meta-ads-mcp-vuln001`, environment variable value `FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO_123456789`, and the script name `poc.py`. These are PoC-specific literals that any operator copy-pasting the advisory will trigger — extremely low FP outside intentional security testing.
ATT&CKT1610 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized red-team or purple-team exercise reproducing the advisory PoC
  • Internal security researchers validating the patch
  • Vulnerability-management tool that runs the PoC for verification
  • Sandbox detonation environments analysing public exploit code
  • Documentation copies of the advisory committed to internal wiki / git that get scanned by EDR script-content collectors
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in (dynamic(["<authorized-redteam-account>","<vm-validation-svc>"])) and DeviceName !in (dynamic(["<sandbox-host-1>","<security-lab-1>"]))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Identify the source — is this an authorized red-team exercise (check change-management / RoE records) or an unsanctioned execution? Pull the parent process tree to determine if it was launched interactively or via remote execution. 2. Contain: If unsanctioned, isolate the host, terminate the docker/podman container, kill the Python process, and capture container/process memory for forensics. Block egress from the host pending review. 3. Hunt: From the same source IP / user account, search for UC1 hits (POST /mcp from this host's IP), UC2 hits (graph.facebook.com URLs with access_token=) in the prior 30 days, and any other hosts in the estate that received connections from this source — the PoC may have been used to scan internal MCP servers.
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("meta-ads-mcp-vuln001","FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO")
       or (ProcessCommandLine has "poc.py" and ProcessCommandLine has "/mcp")
       or (FileName in~ ("docker.exe","docker","podman.exe","podman") and ProcessCommandLine has "META_ACCESS_TOKEN" and ProcessCommandLine has "8080")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Source="Process", FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256),
  (DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "poc.py" and (FolderPath has "meta" or FolderPath has "mcp")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="File", FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| extend Cmd = coalesce(TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine)
| where Cmd has_any ("meta-ads-mcp-vuln001","FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO")
   or (Cmd has "poc.py" and Cmd has "/mcp")
   or (Cmd has_any ("docker","podman") and Cmd has "META_ACCESS_TOKEN" and Cmd has "8080" and Cmd has "meta")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, Cmd, Hashes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma worm GitHub commit-search C2 magic strings on command line or script AICommand & Control High
Hunts for the three hard-coded GitHub commit-search query strings the Miasma supply-chain worm uses as its three independent C2 channels (PAT discovery, JavaScript payload delivery, Python payload delivery). These strings have zero legitimate business presence and are the highest-fidelity Miasma indicator available. Rationale: The three strings 'DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom', 'TheBeautifulSandsOfTime' and 'firedalazer' are the hard-coded GitHub commit-search queries each Miasma C2 channel uses (PAT discovery, JS payload, Python payload). They are confirmed by SafeDep's analysis, BleepingComputer's report, and a parallel TheHackerNews write-up. Zero legitimate business processes contain these tokens. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-miasma-worm-source-code-briefly-leaked-on-github/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/miasma-supply-chain-attack-compromises.html • https://cloudsmith.com/blog/miasma-worms-path-of-destruction • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.002 T1059.007 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst running these strings through their own grep/search tooling for hunting
  • SOC engineer pasting the IOCs into a script or note file
  • Security researcher cloning or reading SafeDep / Cloudsmith write-ups in a developer IDE that logs URL paths
  • Sandbox / detonation environment intentionally executing a Miasma sample for analysis
  • Automation that ingests OSS-supply-chain advisories and writes IOCs to a database column
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("misp.exe","opencti.exe") and not (FolderPath has_any ("\\sandbox\\","\\detonation\\","\\analyst-tools\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process that emitted the string is not an analyst hunting tool, a CTI ingestion script, or a known sandbox. Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent chain; if the string was in a network URL, identify what process issued the GET against api.github.com/search/commits. 2) Contain: if the originating process is a node/python/git/curl invocation on a developer machine or CI runner, isolate the host from network, revoke any GitHub PATs and SSH keys cached on it, and rotate npm/PyPI/RubyGems publish tokens and JFrog Artifactory credentials owned by that user. 3) Hunt: search 30d for the same three strings org-wide; pivot on the parent process and SHA256 to find sibling executions; review the developer's git push history for npm/PyPI/RubyGems package versions published in the last 7d for unexpected new releases or postinstall scripts.
let MiasmaC2 = dynamic(["DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom","TheBeautifulSandsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2) or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, Source = "Process";
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.github.com","github.com")
    | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName = InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256 = InitiatingProcessSHA256, Source = strcat("Net:", RemoteUrl);
union ProcHits, NetHits
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| order by Timestamp desc
let MiasmaC2 = dynamic(["DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom","TheBeautifulSandsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
let From4688 = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source = "4688";
let FromAsim = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2) or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername, NewProcessName = TargetProcessName, CommandLine = TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName = ActingProcessName, Source = "ASIM";
union From4688, FromAsim
| where Account !endswith "$"
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma supply-chain worm leaked repo clone, install or fetch AIDelivery High
Hunts for git clone / npm install / pip install / curl / wget operations that reference the briefly-public 'Miasma-Open-Source-Release' GitHub repositories which leaked the worm's source on 2026-06-08. A match means the host has either ingested the leaked toolkit or is being staged with it. Rationale: 'Miasma-Open-Source-Release' is the exact repository slug SafeDep and BleepingComputer report appeared on GitHub from 2026-06-08 hosting the leaked toolkit. The string is uniquely tied to Miasma and would only surface in dev-tool command lines or proxy URLs when a host is cloning, installing or downloading the leaked source. Cross-checked via SafeDep, BleepingComputer and TheRegister. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-miasma-worm-source-code-briefly-leaked-on-github/ • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074 • https://cloudsmith.com/blog/miasma-worms-path-of-destruction

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Web.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal threat-intel team intentionally cloning the leaked repo into a sandbox for analysis
  • Security researcher fetching the source on a developer workstation for write-up
  • SOAR / TIP ingesting OSS advisory feeds and storing the repo URL as an IOC string
  • Vulnerability scanner or SCA tool fingerprinting against known-malicious repo names
  • Blue-team CTF or training environment seeding the toolkit deliberately
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has_any ("\\sandbox\\", "\\detonation\\", "\\malware-analysis\\", "\\threat-intel\\") and FolderPath !has_any ("\\sandbox\\", "\\detonation\\", "\\malware-analysis\\", "\\threat-intel\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user and parent process that issued the clone/install/fetch — confirm it is not a sanctioned analyst sandbox or CTI ingestion job. Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and any subsequent npm/pip postinstall script execution from the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any node/python child processes spawned within 1 hour of the clone, revoke GitHub PATs and SSH keys cached on it, and rotate npm/PyPI/RubyGems/Artifactory publish tokens belonging to the user. 3) Hunt: search 30d for the three Miasma C2 commit-search strings (see related UC) on the same host and across the org; review the user's recent package publishes for unexpected versions; check GitHub Actions workflows in any repo they touched for newly-added steps referencing untrusted secrets or external scripts.
let MiasmaRepo = "Miasma-Open-Source-Release";
let DevTools = dynamic(["git.exe","npm.exe","node.exe","pip.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","git","npm","node","pip","python","python3","curl","wget"]);
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName in~ (DevTools) or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (DevTools)
    | where ProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo or InitiatingProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, Source = "Process";
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl contains MiasmaRepo
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "Network";
union isfuzzy=true ProcHits, NetHits
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| order by Timestamp desc
let MiasmaRepo = "Miasma-Open-Source-Release";
let From4688 = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source = "4688";
let FromAsim = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo or TargetProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername, NewProcessName = TargetProcessName, CommandLine = TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName = ActingProcessName, Source = "ASIM";
let FromProxy = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL contains MiasmaRepo or DestinationHostName contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = SourceHostName, Account = SourceUserName, NewProcessName = "", CommandLine = RequestURL, ParentProcessName = "", Source = "Proxy";
union From4688, FromAsim, FromProxy
| where Account !endswith "$"
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Miasma Supply Chain Worm Leaked Repository Reference
id: 5f3c8a91-2b6d-4e7a-9f1c-8d5e3a2b4c7e
description: Detects clone, install, fetch or curl/wget references to the 'Miasma-Open-Source-Release' repositories which briefly leaked the Miasma supply-chain worm source on GitHub starting 2026-06-08.
references:
  - https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-miasma-worm-source-code-briefly-leaked-on-github/
  - https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/11
tags:
  - attack.t1195.001
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains: 'Miasma-Open-Source-Release'
  condition: selection
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon OR source:windows.security OR source:linux.auditd OR source:windows.defender) (@CommandLine:(*Miasma-Open-Source-Release* OR *miasma-open-source-release* OR *MIASMA-OPEN-SOURCE-RELEASE*) OR @process.command_line:(*Miasma-Open-Source-Release* OR *miasma-open-source-release* OR *MIASMA-OPEN-SOURCE-RELEASE*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/(git|npm|node|pip|python3?|curl|wget|powershell|pwsh)(\.exe)?$/i
| CommandLine=/Miasma-Open-Source-Release/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process_name) as process_name values(Processes.process) as process values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent_process_name values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("git.exe","npm.exe","node.exe","pip.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","git","npm","node","pip","python","python3","curl","wget")) AND Processes.process="*Miasma-Open-Source-Release*" by Processes.dest Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process_name) as process_name values(Processes.process) as process values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent_process_name values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("git.exe","npm.exe","node.exe","pip.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","git","npm","node","pip","python","python3","curl","wget")) AND Processes.process="*Miasma-Open-Source-Release*" by Processes.dest Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |
    User-driven consent to a third-party OAuth application — illicit-
    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic

references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'

falsepositives:

level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

            - '\rundll32.exe'

            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] FireAnt Metakit updater spawning unexpected interpreter/LOLBin children (supply-chain payload exec)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — OceanLotus: From external espionage to domestic targeting
Installation. Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER C2 network communication (known domains/IPs) · [LLM] OceanLotus Denis/SOUNDBITE DNS tunneling — high-entropy long subdomain bursts · [LLM] OceanLotus PHOREAL ICMP C&C beaconing from workstations · [LLM] OceanLotus WINDSHIELD proxy bypass — direct outbound HTTP(S) from non-browser process · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER C2 network communication (known domains/IPs) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for outbound network connections or DNS resolutions to the specific SPECTRALVIPER C&C infrastructure documented by ESET across the FireAnt supply-chain campaign and the infrastructure/transport corporate intrusion (Oct 2024 – Mar 2026). Targets both Falcon-observed connection events and DNS resolutions to the named domains. Rationale: All six C2 domains (financemachinelearning.com, gatewayrvcenter.com, coachcybersecurity.com, mxprodesign.com, power-sync-services.com, leadingfilipinoteams.com) and eight IPs (139.162.11.152, 142.91.98.77, 139.180.128.42, 139.99.33.239, 166.88.77.186, 103.119.47.104, 38.60.245.37, 194.68.26.241) come directly from the ESET WeLiveSecurity write-up's IOC tables. These overlap with the SPECTRALVIPER infrastructure first publicly documented by Elastic Security Labs in 2023, and ESET explicitly notes financemachinelearning[.]com was the stable-iteration C&C for the FireAnt supply-chain stage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0050/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TI sandboxing platforms (Joe Sandbox, ANY.RUN agents) detonating OceanLotus samples against live infrastructure
  • Red-team exercises explicitly replaying SPECTRALVIPER C2 against the corporate range
  • Security researchers / DFIR teams resolving the domains for passive DNS pivots from internal hosts
  • Threat-intel feeds occasionally re-querying domains during enrichment lookups
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("joeboxserver.exe","sandboxie-rpcss.exe","vmsrvc.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm hit against passive DNS + WHOIS history for the IOC; pull the InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine of the host process; correlate with EmailEvents and UrlClickEvents on the same DeviceId/AccountName in the prior 24h for the likely delivery vector. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the device with Defender Live Response, block the IOC at the egress proxy/firewall, force-rotate the user's credentials and revoke active sessions/tokens, snapshot memory before reimage. Step 3 — Hunt: search SHA1 list (UC3) across the estate, run the FireAnt updater hunt (UC2) if any host had the FireAnt Metakit client, look for parallel infrastructure overlap on registrar/ASN, and scope SPECTRALVIPER persistence (Run keys, scheduled tasks, services) on adjacent hosts in the same AD site.

FireAnt Metakit updater spawning unexpected interpreter/LOLBin children (supply-chain payload exec) AIDelivery High
Hunts for the FireAnt Metakit Vietnamese stock-trading client (the compromised software ESET says delivered SPECTRALVIPER via trojanized updates Oct 2025–Mar 2026) acting as parent for unusual interpreter or LOLBin children. The legitimate FireAnt updater should drop signed binaries only; spawning powershell/cmd/rundll32/regsvr32 or writing unsigned executables into AppData is the supply-chain detonation step. Rationale: Pivots on the article's explicit naming of FireAnt Metakit as the compromised stock-trading client whose update server delivered SPECTRALVIPER between Oct 2025 and Mar 2026. The legitimate updater process has no business spawning interpreters/LOLBins; ESET notes the malicious update either reused old SPECTRALVIPER samples (first iteration) or fetched fresh stages over an API request (stable iteration), both of which need an exec sink. Image binary name 'FireAnt'/'Metakit' is the unique anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.001 T1218.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • FireAnt support engineers running diagnostic PowerShell against installed clients
  • IT helpdesk using cmd.exe shims to reinstall the updater
  • Endpoint software-asset agents invoking certutil to fetch HTTPS resources from the FireAnt install dir
  • Vietnamese MSP investigation/cleanup activity post-disclosure
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--diagnose", "--repair", "/uninstall") and AccountName has_any ("helpdesk", "support", "sccm"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: capture the parent FireAnt binary's SHA256 and signing cert; verify against FireAnt's published current installer hash and look for prior FileCreate events writing the updater. Pull the child process command line and follow-on DeviceNetworkEvents within 10 minutes. Step 2 — Contain: isolate host, kill the descendant process tree, quarantine the FireAnt install directory contents, block C2 IOCs from UC1, and rotate the user's AD password + revoke sessions. Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate all hosts in the org with FireAnt Metakit installed (DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory), check for the SPECTRALVIPER hash list (UC3) and C2 connections (UC1), pivot the executed payload SHA256 across all endpoints, and inspect FireAnt update.log / metadata for unsigned/mismatched updates between Oct 2025 and Mar 2026.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(180d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("FireAnt", "fireant", "Metakit", "metakit")
    or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\FireAnt\", @"\Metakit\")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","msbuild.exe","installutil.exe")
    or (FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\Temp\") and FileName endswith ".exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA1, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(180d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("FireAnt","fireant","Metakit","metakit")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, SHA256

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(180d) and EventID == 4688

| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")

Known SPECTRALVIPER / OceanLotus SHA1 hash execution or write AIInstallation High
Direct hash-based detection for the 20 SPECTRALVIPER and OceanLotus loader samples ESET published across both the infrastructure/transport corporate intrusion and the FireAnt supply-chain campaign. Catches the binaries on execution (ProcessEvents) and on disk drop (FileEvents) — including DLL side-load components for which only the loader runs as a child. Rationale: The 20 SHA1 hashes are pulled verbatim from the ESET IOC tables and include both the first-iteration (re-used older sample) and stable-iteration (heavily obfuscated, fresh) SPECTRALVIPER builds, plus the loaders observed against the infrastructure/transport corporation. Hash-based detection is the highest-fidelity catch we can ship; pairing process + file + image-load tables ensures we catch side-load components that never execute as a main process. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1086/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1055 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analysts uploading samples to internal sandbox/EDR test rings
  • CrowdStrike/Defender Threat Experts pivot-hunts touching the binary on lab hosts
  • Incident-response handlers staging IOCs into Velociraptor / DFIR triage VMs
  • TI feed cron jobs writing the hash to local disk via VirusTotal-CLI
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has_any ("-SANDBOX", "-MALLAB", "-DFIRVM")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm SHA1 vs. published ESET IOC and pull the parent process chain, original drop path, and signing certificate; check whether the host is in an analyst/sandbox tag pool to rule out test detonations. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host, kill the process + descendants, quarantine the file system-wide (Defender Live Response: `quarantine`), block the hash at AV policy. Rotate the user's credentials. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot the parent process across the estate, search for the C2 IOCs (UC1) and the FireAnt supply-chain hunt (UC2) for adjacent hosts; expand to SHA256 once derived; check 365-day file-creation events for prior dormant drops; review scheduled tasks / Run keys / services on the host for SPECTRALVIPER's orchestration persistence.

OceanLotus Denis/SOUNDBITE DNS tunneling — high-entropy long subdomain bursts AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for DNS-tunneling C2 behaviour consistent with OceanLotus's Denis (SOUNDBITE) backdoor described in the article. Targets endpoints emitting bursts of TXT/A queries with unusually long, high-entropy labels — the encoded-payload shape Denis uses to multiplex C&C in/out of DNS. Pairs query-shape statistics with originating process to keep noise down. Rationale: The article explicitly names Denis (aka SOUNDBITE) as 'implementing DNS tunneling for C&C communications' as part of the OceanLotus arsenal. The detection targets the canonical DNS-tunneling shape (label length >=30, high entropy, burst over 5m) without naming a specific suffix — Denis rotates parent zones, so the count-per-zone aggregation is what survives infrastructure changes. Statistical/threshold logic, no clean Sigma equivalent. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0050/ • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0186/
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1572 T1132.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Antivirus / EDR cloud-lookup traffic (e.g. Symantec Insight, McAfee GTI) which encodes file metadata into long subdomains
  • Microsoft SmartScreen / Office click-time URL telemetry to *.events.data.microsoft.com
  • Outlook autodiscover and Office365 long-suffix telemetry domains
  • CDN sharded asset hostnames (Akamai, Cloudflare workers) using long random labels
Suppression filter
| where Parent !endswith "events.data.microsoft.com" and Parent !endswith ".trendmicro.com" and Parent !endswith ".symantec.com" and Parent !endswith ".mcafee.com" and Parent !endswith ".akadns.net"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the parent zone and run a WHOIS / passive-DNS lookup; pull the InitiatingProcessFileName + commandline that initiated the queries and verify it's not a known AV/EDR cloud-lookup channel. Step 2 — Contain: sinkhole or block the parent zone at the recursive DNS resolver; isolate the host if the process is unsigned or unfamiliar; capture a memory dump for malware reversal. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot the parent zone across all DNS logs to find lateral compromise, search the SPECTRALVIPER hash list (UC3) on the host, and review for ICMP and direct-outbound activity (UC5/UC6) suggesting other OceanLotus protocol tunnels on the same victim.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
| extend Query = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).Query)
| where isnotempty(Query)
| extend Label = tostring(split(Query, ".")[0])
| extend LabelLen = strlen(Label)
| extend Parent = strcat_array(array_slice(split(Query, "."), 1, -1), ".")
| where LabelLen >= 30
| summarize QueryCount = count(), UniqueLabels = dcount(Label), MaxLabelLen = max(LabelLen), SampleQuery = any(Query)
          by bin(Timestamp, 5m), DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, Parent
| where QueryCount > 30 and UniqueLabels > 20
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where QueryType in ("A","AAAA","TXT")
| extend Label = tostring(split(Name, ".")[0])
| extend LabelLen = strlen(Label)
| extend Parent = strcat_array(array_slice(split(Name, "."), 1, -1), ".")
| where LabelLen >= 30
| summarize QueryCount = count(), UniqueLabels = dcount(Label), MaxLabelLen = max(LabelLen), SampleQuery = any(Name)
          by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m), Computer, ClientIP, Parent
| where QueryCount > 30 and UniqueLabels > 20
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22 @QueryName:/^[a-zA-Z0-9+\-_=]{30,}\..+/
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| LabelLen := length(DomainName)
| firstLabel := regex("^(?<lbl>[^.]+)\\.", field=DomainName, strict=false)
| firstLabelLen := length(lbl)
| firstLabelLen >= 30
| parent := replace("^[^.]+\\.", with="", field=DomainName)
| bucket(field=_time, span=5m)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, parent, _bucket], function=[count(as=qcount), count(distinct=true, field=DomainName, as=unique_q), max(field=firstLabelLen, as=max_label)])
| qcount > 30
| unique_q > 20
| sort(field=_bucket, order=desc)
